utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. All the accused are present. I notice the absence of Mr. Meek. And the prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Mitchell and Mr. Thayer. Yes. You would have noticed the absence of Judge Kwon. He's on official business which I authorised, because we had planned to finish the Prosecution case on the 1st and then it was a point of no return, and so he won't be with us for the rest of the week. So we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Any preliminaries? Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, on Friday, after the Court's oral decision in relation to the calling of Witness 195, I indicated, on behalf of my client, that we needed some time to consider the issue of certification. We do wish to apply for certification of that decision. My oral submission will take no more than five minutes. I will make it at whatever juncture today the Court feels is convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Let me consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse, you may proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I turn to the criteria under the Rule itself, in effect these are the matters that we would wish to pursue on appeal in relation to this matter: Firstly, the failure of the Trial Chamber to give proper time to the Defence of General Gvero to reply to the Prosecution motion in the first place. In particular, by reason of that failure, the fact that it prevented the Defence researching fully and properly factual and legal matters that arose, in particular the issue of prejudice to the accused by reason of the lateness of the motion and the lateness of the addition of the name to the 65 ter witness list. So far as the decision itself is concerned, the failure by the Trial Chamber to apply the law properly in relation to the issue of prejudice and, in any event, in other words, in the alternative, the wrong use of discretion in relation to the same issue, namely, prejudice. Thirdly, the failure of the Trial Chamber to allow the Defence proper time to prepare for the witness prior to her testimony, particularly bearing in mind the practice applied in this case hitherto in relation to all or virtually all previous witnesses who have given their evidence. And, finally, the over-slavish adherence by the Trial Chamber to the existing schedule, to the grave potential detriment to my client. So far as the Rule itself is concerned, as is well-known - and I'm not going to spend very long on this at all - there are two hurdles that an applicant needs to overcome. So far as the first hurdle is concerned, it's either that the issue would affect significantly the fair and expeditious conduct of the proceedings or the outcome of the trial. It's really the words "outcome of the trial" that we rely upon here. As has been accepted by both the Prosecution and the Defence, and indeed the decision itself used the words "important point," this is an important issue, and as such it is beyond doubt one which we submit would significantly affect the outcome of the trial, and therefore would benefit from a resolution by the Appeals Chamber. Of course, there's a second limb that we also need to overcome, and that is in relation to an immediate resolution by the Appeals Chamber may materially advance the proceedings. Firstly, we emphasise the rule "may" in the Rule, so far as that is concerned. Secondly, so far as the immediate resolution is concerned, it's important because it clearly is going to affect how the Defence intends and will address the issue when it comes to our turn. Our consideration would be completely different, depending on whether or not this particular witness gives her evidence. And we can test this another way, and that is in relation to our application for the recall of certain Prosecution witnesses. The Defence have stated categorically and have demonstrated, in fact, that they weren't going to seek the recall of the witnesses on the evidence on this point hitherto. However, the Defence have now said they will seek the recall of these witnesses. An immediate resolution by the Appeals Chamber would materially advance the proceedings in that regard, because it would clarify whether those witnesses need to be recalled, and therefore the proceedings would be much clearer. And in particular, in short, we say that if this important issue was ruled upon at this particular juncture, namely, whether this important piece of corroborative evidence should be called or not, it would clearly affect the outcome of the trial and may undoubtedly materially affect -- advance the proceedings. In conclusion, could we submit this, Your Honour, and I know I've said it before and I'm going to sound like a broken gramophone here, but I make no apologies for it, extraneous considerations in relation to scheduling and time restraints are exactly that, extraneous, and they should play no part in the Trial Chamber's decision under Rule 73, which makes no reference to scheduling considerations. Those are our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Josse. Mr. McCloskey or Mr. Thayer, would you like to respond? Very briefly, please, not much longer than Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you and Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone. It will certainly be brief, because I wasn't aware that we would be orally addressing this this afternoon. Nevertheless, suffice it to say that it's the Prosecution's position that the Defence has met neither prong of Rule 73, and in particular I note the absence of any reference to the Trial Chamber's fair and reasonable approach to this new evidence, which entails permitting the technical reopening of the Prosecution's case prior to any Defence case presented by the Gvero team, ultimately of course depending on the outcome of the 98 bis proceedings. That measure -- that measure that the Trial Chamber imposed in its oral decision of last Friday, I think, satisfies all of these concerns. It permits this investigation to be concluded, should the Defence in the end think that that testimony is even worth for it to bring out. That avenue that the Court laid open, I think, defeats any of the grounds upon which my friend is seeking certification under Rule 73. And once again, despite the prior notice of this issue, dating all the way back to the first week of November, my friend has not presented one wit of evidence either or authority in law or in fact about how he is going to be prejudiced. It is speculative. He referred to grave potential detriment. There has been no -- no authority cited to this Court at all at any point on that issue. For that reason, I think the certification motion, respectfully, should be denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. We'll come back to you with our decision at the earliest. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Judges. Good afternoon, colleagues. Mr. President, there are two issues I would like to briefly address the Trial Chamber. The first one relates to the admissibility of Exhibits 685 and 686, which are the narratives prepared by the witness Richard Butler to which I referred last Friday. Mr. President, some of the Defence team and possibly all Defence teams will be filing a joint motion challenging the admissibility of the narratives prepared by Richard Butler, and due to the fact that -- or due to the duration of his testimony and the need to refer to this testimony in our motion, I hereby apply and seek leave from the Trial Chamber to exceed the normal word limit and to file a motion not exceeding 6.000 words. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to respond to that, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would object to the exceeding the word limit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Permission is granted, Mr. Bourgon. However, I'm sure Mr. Josse will agree with us, this is certainly not an extraneous matter. It's in your own interest, considering the proximity of the Rule 98 bis to file this with the utmost clarity so that we can do our utmost to decide it in good time for you to know whether these reports or findings would be taken into consideration in the course of the Rule 98 bis exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have been coordinating over the weekend, and this motion can be filed today, probably, but we wanted to be sure about the asking permission to exceed the word limit before the motion is filed, in accordance with the practice direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That permission is granted. That's the first one. You had a second one?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The second topic, Mr. President, deals with what the Trial Chamber ruled last week concerning the Prosecution's 92 quater motion, that the impact thereof would not be considered for the Rule 98 bis purposes. I would just like to know, Mr. President, is: Can we expect a ruling in writing on this issue? And the reason I ask is simply because there might be the need to call some further witnesses for further cross-examination, and this has not been addressed in the oral decision that was given by the Chamber on Friday. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we made our position clear. For the purpose of Rule 98 bis, it's as if we don't have on our table that motion at all. In other words, there is no 92 quater evidence that are in the record and that will be referred to by the Trial Chamber in reaching its decision. However, yes, of course there will be a decision later on. I mean, this decision that we are taking now, in other words, to keep that material out of the records for the purpose of Rule 98 bis, we have decided it. I don't think we need to put that in writing. You have our word. But then there will be a written decision on the motion itself, after of course having received your responses which you will take the normal time. I mean, we are not restricting the time limits for the filing of those motions. File them within the time limit and then we will decide it. We will obviously not decide it before the Rule 98 bis exercise, because the purpose of our previous decision was precisely that, that we will give this matter, which is of importance, our absolute attention, and then we'll decide it later on, when we are ready. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we bring in the witness, Mr. McCloskey and members of the Defence teams, I refer you to Prosecution motion of the 31st of January, seeking leave to amend the 65 ter exhibit list with two exhibits pertaining to this witness. There are not going to be any protective measures for this witness, are there? Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, there are not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So Witness 192, Tomic, anyway. Is there any objection on the part of any of the Defence teams? All right, thank you. So the motion is granted, Mr. McCloskey or Mr. Thayer. Who will be leading this witness? I take it Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we bring in the witness ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In relation to the documents arising from Butler's testimony, my original idea was to ask you, very briefly, whether you anticipate a long debate or not, in the absence of which my intention was to proceed today with the tendering process. I was not anticipating, of course, what Mr. Bourgon stated earlier on, and that brings us to the conclusion that it's better if we delayed the issue of the Butler documents until we're finished with these three witnesses, which would leave us then with the motion and any other matters that may be raised by way of objection to the tendering of documents from both sides. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and that sounds fine. But just to make it clear, especially if there's a motion filed, we have our big list of Butler exhibits. We also have his narratives and his command reports on CD that are hyperlinked to the cited documents in them, and so we always offer Mr. Butler's reports as well as his various footnotes and citations, because without them the report doesn't make as much sense. And so that's the matter at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. McCloskey. But considering the procedure that we have adopted from the beginning of this case, there should be no problems, because where there are objections that cannot be resolved or which are tied, intrinsically tied to the motion that we are expecting, then we can always MIF -- or MFI and admit the rest and we can proceed, and then for the purpose of the Rule 98 bis exercise you will know exactly where you stand. So we will deal with it in the practical way that we have adopted so far. So you don't -- please don't expect any particular complications or problems. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to confirm that the joint motion being prepared addresses solely Exhibit 685 and 686, which are the narratives, and not the other documents. However, regarding the issue just raised by my colleague, we will object to the handing over of such a CD assistance unless my colleague can establish a clear link between every document used -- or that the links with that CD with a Rule 65 ter number. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The 65 ter number that links these documents is the 65 ter number for the narrative and the command reports. They are clearly on notice, have been on notice forever. These documents have always been put into the evidence in the other trial. It's not an issue of notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, let's not lose more time on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just one other thing. We had the large-size maps related to the small size that we had provided you, and we have those now. I don't know if you want those, or we can always bring them back, if need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You're about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, our Rules require that you solemnly declare that you will be speaking the truth. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of the solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [The witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, I am hopeful that we will finish with you today. Mr. Thayer will go first, and then he will be followed by all or some of the Defence teams on cross-examination. Your duty is not to make a distinction between Prosecution and Defence and to answer each question that is put to you as precisely and as truthfully as possible. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just ask you, if you could, just move your chair just a little bit closer to the microphone, and that way it will pick up everything you say.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, would you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Milenko Tomic, son of Djordje.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how old are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of July, 1948.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you please tell the Trial Chamber where you were born and raised?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I was born in Tuzla, and I live in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how long have you lived in Zvornik, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Sixty years.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you identify yourself as a Bosnian Serb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Please tell the Trial Chamber what you do for a living.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I'm a driver of trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you work for a particular company, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I work for the company of Metalno in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how long have you been a driver for the Metalno company in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Thirty-nine years.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn your attention to the war and ask you what kind of duties you performed during the war.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I was a driver, and for a while I was at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And as a driver, sir, and, for that matter, when you were at the front line, do you recall which battalion you were a member of?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: While I was at the front line, I don't know. I was periodically a driver, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you were driving, as part of your military duties, do you recall which battalion you were attached to?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: That was the Standard barracks. That's where I belonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And just to clarify this one point, sir, may we have 65 ter 3227 on e-court, please. Do you see a document in front of you, sir, on the computer?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down just a little bit, you told us your father's name was Djordje?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There's an entry at line 24 --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- that refers to a Milenko Tomic, son of Djordje, and do you see the name "Metalno" there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now if we could scroll back up to the top of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see that there's a reference to the R Battalion in the heading there, near the date of December 15th?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says, yes, in the top part of the document, at 0800 hours, and above that it says "The R Company."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Or "The R Battalion." Do you see that, sir? It may be a translation issue.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My question is very simple, sir. During your military service, did you ever hear a reference to the R Battalion? And if so, do you know what that "R" stood for?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: When we were under work obligation, we would be assigned to the barracks there to work for the army. That was the R Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And just one last question on this. Do you recall what that letter "R" stood for? What did that abbreviation refer to, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I think that whenever we were under work obligation and working for a company, we would be asked to report to the barracks to the R Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter adds the witness said "to the military post there."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Trial Chamber, please, the procedure or how you would receive assignments from the Standard barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: When we were at the barracks, in the morning, if a trip had to be made, one received a travel order and fuel. The boss, meaning the person charged with these tasks, would issue us this assignment and we'd be off.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And let's just back up for one second. Most of the time, it's fair to say, you were permitted to work at your company, Metalno; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, depending on the times, depending on the needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how were you notified, when you were at your company, that your presence was required at the Standard barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: For the most part, it was either by a telephone or a courier would come to the company, and then the bosses, who would be in touch with them, would let us know that we had to report to the barracks, to the Standard barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you arrived at the Standard barracks, sir, to whom would you report?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: We'd report to the office of Radislav Pantic, where the drivers would normally stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you know Mr. Pantic before the war, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him. He worked with me in the same company.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you know what position he held in the army, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think he was the head of transports. He'd assign different vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when you reported to Mr. Pantic at Standard, was there any particular form or document which he would give you before you set out on your assignment?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Only a travel order, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during the war, sir, when you arrived at Standard to receive your orders, did anyone other than Mr. Pantic issue these travel orders to you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Sometimes somebody else would issue them, but most of the time it was Pantic who did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. I want to turn your attention to a particular day and to a particular assignment you received, and it's no surprise to anyone here what that was. And I know and I can see that this isn't easy for you, and I just want to ask you to, if you can, take your time when you tell the Court what happened that day. And, sir, if at any time you feel like you need a break for any reason, please do not hesitate to say so. Okay? And I'll start my questions in a moment. I just want to make sure you understand that.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Please, sir, tell the Court about this assignment you received on this particular day. And if you remember the day, please tell the Court, and just take us from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Truth to tell, I don't recall the date. But based on what you -- what I received, the travel order, I was able to see. It was on that day that I received my travel order from Radislav Pantic and I set off. When I arrived in the place called Pilica, I didn't come across anyone at the centre there. I set off toward Kula, another small settlement not far away from there. I was supposed to report to somebody else there, but I -- again I found no one. I returned to Pilica. On the way out of Pilica, along the main road, that's some 100 metres away from downtown Pilica, I came across a soldier who pulled me over and told me that I should report outside the dom there. I followed him and reached the dom. He told me to park the vehicle next to a side door that was just there by the dom. Having parked there, I went with him to a nearby house, where there was a lady who offered us a cup of coffee. In fact, he had told me that we should have a cup of coffee there. I had a cup of coffee and a couple of shots of rakija, of brandy, as well. After a while, the man joined me again and said that we would be able to set off in half an hour's time. I joined him without noticing anything in particular. I saw that the sides of the truck, the tarpaulin had been lowered without having been tied, in fact, and he said, "We're going up there." I asked him what it was that we were driving there, and he, after some hesitation, said that we were driving dead bodies. Once we reached that place up there, what's it called, Branjevo, he said that we should park there. As I was approaching that area, I observed some individuals in civilian clothes. I parked there. He then told me that there were some cattle barns there, that we should spend a while there. We came upon some workers who were feeding the cattle there. I lingered with them for a while, had a couple of shots of brandy, and talked to them. Later on, on my way back, I didn't notice anything in particular. I got into the truck, and he said that we should leave. I returned to the very same spot where I was earlier on, parked the vehicle there, and he took me once more to that lady, to sit there for a while and have some more brandy. I engaged in a conversation with her, but she never said anything about what was going on. Roughly half an hour later, the man rejoined us and said that we should leave once more. As we were on our way up there, I asked him again, "Well, how much of it is there?" He really didn't tell me anything. As we reached the area up there and approached a site, I saw some corpses lying farther away. I parked the vehicle in the reverse and went to the barn again where I was earlier on. Around a half hour passed, and in the meanwhile I had a couple of shots of brandy again. We went back down there, and as we approached an intersection, we were stopped. A soldier standing there told us, "You're off the hook. You're not needed anymore." And at that point, he told me one, "One of the sides at the back of your truck has not been lowered." I got out of the truck, lowered the side, and then headed for Zvornik, leaving them behind. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. I just want to follow up with a couple of questions about what you've just told us. When Mr. Pantic gave you the travel order this day, did he tell you where you were to go?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, he said that I should set out for Pilica and then Kula, and that I was going to pick up the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when you encountered this soldier, you stated that you had gone to Kula and then to Pilica, and when you were stopped by this particular soldier, sir, can you describe anything to the Trial Chamber about this soldier's appearance, his uniform, his age, anything at all about this soldier that you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, I think the soldier had the old uniform on of the former Yugoslav People's Army. He was perhaps some 30 years of age. I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the purpose of -- the ultimate purpose of the question put to you by Mr. Thayer was intended to elicit from you anything this soldier was wearing on his uniform that could identify his rank or the unit to which he belonged. Did he have any insignia on the uniform that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he didn't have any insignia or ranks on the uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And during these times, did you ever or had you ever seen other soldiers wearing the same kind of uniform, that is, the old JNA uniform, or was it this -- was this the first time that you saw someone wearing that kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think -- well, I had that old uniform on whenever I was doing a job of work or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So just to follow up on His Honour's question, how would you describe, if at all, if you can, the purpose of the uniform that you saw? Was there some special purpose that you associate with the type of uniform that you saw this soldier wearing?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, probably these were uniforms one would wear when doing physical work on construction sites, whilst carrying construction materials and stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, during this first trip to the dom at Pilica, sir, or during your second trip, did you see any other soldiers present in the area, in addition to this one that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: There were some perhaps six soldiers wearing the same uniform, without any insignia, who were working. I didn't see anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you described this one soldier who accompanied you on these trips as being perhaps in his 30s. Do you recall the general age of the other soldiers that you saw around the Pilica dom when you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: The other ones were older than him, between 50 and 52 years of age. He was the youngest among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You described this door at which you parked your truck at the dom as being a side door, sir. Do you remember how you physically parked your truck at that door? In what direction?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I parked it slant-wise, and I drew a sketch of it, slant-wise with the back side facing the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, on this second trip that you took to Branjevo, when you saw the bodies, can you describe in just a little bit more detail how it was that you came to see these bodies, and can you describe for the Trial Chamber approximately how many you saw? We know that you weren't counting them, but can you describe, in general terms, how many bodies you saw there at Branjevo?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: When I got out of the vehicle, I saw them lying on the ground next to the back side. I don't know how many of them there were; five or ten. I didn't count them. When I saw those civilians eating there, holding a slice of bread and sausage in their hands, I just couldn't bear to watch that. I felt sick and had to get away.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you were told that you weren't needed anymore or that your services weren't needed, where did you go next with your truck?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I drove toward the barracks, and on the way I dropped by some bars, had a couple of shots more, and then finally drove to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Where did you leave the truck, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I left the truck on the parking lot where the trucks were normally left. I left the keys and the travel order in the cab of the truck and went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall being told to do anything with your truck after you had transported these bodies?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: When I closed one of the sides at the intersection there, I realised that the back side of the truck had been all muddied and bloodied over, and I knew I should do something about it. But with all the alcohol that I had drunk earlier on, I wasn't able to do it. I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a few more questions, sir. You referred to a sketch that you drew, and you drew that sketch back in November, when the investigators first met with you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we'll look at the sketch in a moment, but before we do: Do you remember generally what you drew on that sketch?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I drew the main road, the dom, the nearby houses, the entrance, and the parked vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. May we have 65 ter 3226, please. And if we could magnify it just a little bit, please. Great, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see this document in front of you on your screen?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You recognise what that is?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: It's the main road between Zvornik and Bijeljina and the side road which takes you up to the village, the memorial site, and the cultural hall or the dom, as well as the truck, TAM 130.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just going to ask you to explain these just a little bit. You mentioned the Zvornik-Bijeljina road. Is that what's depicted at the bottom of the sketch with the arrow leading from Zvornik, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we look at the left-hand portion of the sketch, you've marked a large rectangle with the initials "DK." What does that stand for, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Dom Kultur or Culture Hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And below that there is a little sort of circle or smaller area you've indicated right below the rectangle of the Dom Kultur. Can you tell us what that is? It looks like --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: The memorial site.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And you've already told us you wrote in "TAM 130" next to where your truck was parked; is that correct? We need an audible -- a "yes" or "no" just so we can pick it up on the transcript, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And I see there's a little "V" with a period on this sketch of the Dom Kultur that you drew. What does that "V" stand for?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you see where you've drawn the truck?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to the left of the truck --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can't we show it to him? Yes, there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see the little --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Right there, sir, there's a little "V" and a period. Can you just tell us what that "V." stands for?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I think I wanted to mark a door there, and I put a "V" with a dot.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we just move across this little sketch, to the right you've drawn another rectangle with the letter "K," "U," and a "C." What is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: "Kuca," "house."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And which house is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Where I went to have coffee and brandy.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And right below that, sir, you drew another rectangle with a couple of initials in there. What is that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: A store.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I think we're done with this exhibit. Oh, and if we could just scroll up a little bit. A little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see some writing in the lower right-hand corner there, a date of November 15th, 2007? Can you tell us what that is there in the corner?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I wrote that, and my signature is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Just one more document to show you, sir. If we could have P00295 on e-court, please. And we'll be looking at page 581 of the original B/C/S, and that would be page 583 of the English translation. But I'd like to work with the B/C/S original, as it's an original document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So no broadcasts. This document is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the document in front of you on your computer?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you just tell the Trial Chamber, generally, what is this type of document that you're looking at?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: It's a travel log. You receive that with the vehicle when you're supposed to carry out some work.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you see, on the right-hand portion of this document, where it says: "Vehicle work log" and then the number "221667;" do you see that, sir? I just want to orient you on the document.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to ask you some questions as we move down, line by line, on this page. Okay? Oh, I'm sorry, can we scroll back up? Not that fast. There is an entry, if we scroll to the right, please, and now we're looking at the very top of the screen on the right-hand side, there's an entry of 15 July until 31 July 1995. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The first date is the date of my arrival in the barracks, and this vehicle log was valid until the 31st of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we look at the line right underneath that, there's a reference to a TAM 130. What is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: It is the type of vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you just describe what kind of vehicle that is, please?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: It's a freight vehicle, six metres in length, metal chassis, 2.3 metres in width, with a tarpaulin.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we go down a couple more lines, there is a little box that refers to the rank, first name and last name. Do you see your name there, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I do. It says "Tomic, Milenko."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And let's move down a little bit to this larger box with a number of columns. And do you see a column that is headed "Date," with a series of dates underneath it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I do. Those are the dates when the vehicle is being refueled. Also specified is the amount of fuel, and then you sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you see the entry for the 17th of July, 1995, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we go all the way to the right, to the last column, there is an entry headed: "Manager's Signature." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we can, let's scroll to the left of this document. I want to show you the left-hand side. And if we can scroll up just a little bit, please, to capture the top. There we go, okay. Now, do you see, on this left-hand portion, an entry for the 17th?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we look in that middle column, where it says: "Condition," what does it say there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: The middle column?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. If you're looking at the line that's number 17, and do you see the column --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- Okay, that says: "Condition" at the very top, do you see the entry on that line 17? Can you read that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I can't. I can't read that. However, I can read where it says: "Signature."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recognise any of those signatures there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I recognise that signature as that of Radislav Pantic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If you would, sir, with Madam Usher's help, I would just ask you to take this pen that's attached to your computer, and if you would circle where you see Mr. Pantic's signature in this column. If you see it more than once, please circle those entries as well.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does he recognise the other signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, did you understand His Honour's question? Do you recognise the other signatures there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, if you would just, on the lower left-hand corner of this document, if you would just place your initials and today's date, which is the 5th of February, 2008.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then we'll save the document and be done with it. And just your initials, too, sir, is fine.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we could save that, please. Okay, thank you. Let's move to the next page of this document, and it will be the next page in both B/C/S and English. And if we could again work with the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, this is my last series of questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could -- that's fine, actually, just where it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to ask you first: Working from left to right -- well, let me back up for a second. Just to orient yourself, this is the flip side of the document we just looked at; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we look at the first column, do you see where it says: "Date"?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: The 17th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. The third column in from the left indicates what, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: The route I drove.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's talk about that, as long as you're -- we're on there. What does it say there, sir, under: "Route" for the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: The first one was for military purposes, Zvornik-Pilica- Kula-Pilica-Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recognise the handwriting in this column number 4 under: "Route"?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Column 4 route, that is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is it your handwriting for every entry there, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: All of it is mine, all of the routes and kilometres, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could scroll over to the -- all the way to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see the final column all the way to the right, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recognise any of the signatures there in that column?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I only recognise Radislav Pantic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And I just ask you again, if you would, to take that pen, and if you would, sir, please circle where you see Mr. Pantic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what does this column indicate? What is its heading, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: "User signature."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could scroll back over all the way to the left, please. We have to sign it. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, if you would please, again put today's date, 5 February 2008, and your initials. Anywhere on the document is fine.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we can save it, we'll be done with it, and then we'll have to scroll over to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, looking back at the column to the far left of this document - thank you, Madam Usher, I think that's it for now - again focusing your attention on that left column where it says: "Date" --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- under the date of 17 July 1995, what is the next entry that you've put in there? What is the date of the next --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: The 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what does that indicate to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: The 20th of July, it means that I drove on that day as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And after this day on the 17th, when you drove to Pilica and Kula, do you recall when it was that you saw Mr. Pantic next?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Three days later, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you saw him the next time, did you say anything to him about this assignment that he'd given you on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I asked him why he had sent me to do that. He never replied or, rather, he said, "Well, I didn't know about it either."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, my last couple of questions here, and I want to just test your recollection a little bit on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think in following the Appellate Chamber's most recent decision on working with a witness's recollection and challenging the recollection, I'm going to ask the Court to permit me to refresh this witness's recollection with a prior statement to test his memory on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's keep this short, Mr. Bourgon, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, any further -- I would just suggest that any further discussion may be outside -- may need to be outside the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then I think the witness can leave the courtroom. We'll hear the submission, and then we'll have the break soon after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon. Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to know which decision of the Appeals Chamber my colleague is referring to. If it's the decision that I have in mind, there's a procedure set in that decision, which is that he must first ask the witness whether the witness remembers what he wants to talk about. It would be useful if we would know exactly the question my colleague intends to ask the witness, as well as the answer he intends to get, and that will allow us to know if the procedure is being followed. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are perfectly right. Basically, I think he's referring to the decision, last week's decision of the Appeals Chamber with regard to impeaching one's own witness, but at this stage I don't think we have arrived at that. We're just dealing, as I see it, at least so far, unless I'm convinced of the contrary or of anything else, that counsel would like to inquire into the possibility of getting the witness -- refreshing the witness's memory in relation to this last answer that he has given, if I understand you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, you do understand me well. However, I do intend, depending on what the answer is, to challenge the credibility, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We come to that at the right stage, I mean, not now. Now, I don't think you need the Trial Chamber's permission to put to the witness a prior statement of his, if the sole purpose of that is to try and refresh his memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Understood. I just wanted to raise it before we went down too far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Appeals Chamber decision doesn't come at this stage. Anyway, shall we have the break now, and in the meantime perhaps even discuss amongst yourselves, because I don't know what your question is going to be, and maybe if you discuss it with counsel, things can work out easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if he can tell us the question, it will be much easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Anyway, we'll have a 25-minute break, and your time is soon over in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President. It's my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Before we took the break, you told us that when you next saw Mr. Pantic, that you complained to him about the assignment, and you said that he told you that he didn't know, either, what you were going to be doing up there. I want to ask you first, sir: Do you recall, back in November, just this past November, when you met with the OTP investigators, do you recall being asked about when you saw Mr. Pantic a few days after the 17th of July; do you recall being asked those questions?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall what you told the investigators, back in November, Mr. Pantic's response to you was when you complained to him about the assignment he had given you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I think that during that conversation, he told me, "I didn't know," and then he turned around and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. But my question to you right now, sir, is, and please focus on the meeting you had with the investigators back in November: Do you remember now exactly what you told the investigators, back in November, Mr. Pantic telling you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I do think that -- well, I think he turned around and left. I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what I'd like to do, sir, is -- we don't have this on e-court, but I have the two pages from your witness interview from back in November, and I'd like to, if we could, maybe put this on the ELMO. Can you see that on your screen, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I don't know about you folks, but I can't see anything on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yeah, we have a blank screen here, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I still can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, to save time, maybe I'll just ask the witness to read what's in front of him into the record. That way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you give him the statement in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: He has the B/C/S in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to save time, if the witness could just read what's marked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see a little orange highlighting at line -- I believe it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I will feel more serene if you show it at least to one or two of the Defence team counsel before --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I've indicated to my friends what the cite is. It's page 24, line 11, through page 25, line 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think you have to raise it up a little bit. Scroll up. Okay, okay, okay, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see that on your screen? The "TB" is the initials of the investigator who was asking you questions, and the "MT" is you answering the questions?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And do you see where you say -- you told him: "Why did you send me there?" And you were asked what was his response. That's at line 16?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you see your answer?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I do. "Why did you send me there?" And then his answer. What can I tell you, what else can I tell you? He turned his back to me and then left. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then the next question is: "Did he even say one word?" And your response was --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: He said nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Then you were asked again, a couple of lines later: "Did he comment somehow?" And do you see your answer: "He just turned and left"?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, he turned and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you see, further down, where the question is: "Did he ask you any questions regarding his task?" And your answer was: "He didn't ask anything." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: What number is that, 27?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you can scroll down just a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said: "Why did you send me there?"

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the next page. Just a little bit further to the top. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There's a question: "Did he ask you any questions regarding his task?" Your answer was: "He didn't ask anything."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The question is: "Just turned around and left?" Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And your answer was: "And then the next order was just -- issued the order and you take it, and he -- that's it. No comment."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We're done with this. Thank you, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, when was the last time you saw or spoke with Mr. Pantic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Before I was to leave for here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Approximately how many days before you were to leave for The Hague, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: A day or two, perhaps. I can't be specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you spoke with Mr. Pantic on this occasion, did you tell him about the fact that you were coming to The Hague soon to give evidence here?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I told him that I was going to go to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: During this conversation, sir, did he tell you anything or say anything to you about the order he gave to you on the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. He told me that he had not known about it, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir, thank you. I don't have any further questions for you at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll say, so that we can save a little time, with the possible exception of Madam Nikolic, I know that nobody else has any questions, bar me, so I will go first, and it may well be that Madam Nikolic has no questions either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Tomic. My name is Peter Haynes, and I represent Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to see if my mathematics is correct. At the time the war started in Bosnia and Herzegovina, you would have been about 44 years of age; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And by July of 1995, you'd have been just short of your 47th birthday; am I correct about that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. Well, you've given us your date of birth as the 30th of July of 1948. We can perhaps all work it out. But from what you tell us, had you by then spent in excess of 20 years working for the same company, Metalno?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I started working for Metalno in 1974, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: For how long of that period of time did you work with Radislav Pantic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I must have worked for at least ten years before that, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what was your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it's not clear, before what? Ten years before what? You said "for at least ten years before that." Before what? Mr. Tomic, look at me. It's me who's asking you the question. Maybe it's the transcript, maybe I didn't understand you well, but Mr. Haynes asked you for how long of that period, that 20-odd years, in other words, did you work with Radislav Pantic, and you said, at least according to our transcript: "I must have worked for at least ten years before that." Before what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the start of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay, that's clearer. Yes, thank you, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and thank you, Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what was your working relationship with Mr. Pantic? Was he, like you, just a driver, or was he your boss in some way?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: He was my boss. He was my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you just a couple of questions about Metalno. Metalno is a company that makes metal construction objects, isn't it, like bridges?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But as part of its operations, it has a fleet or had a fleet of about 17 lorries in 1995, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just so we can clear this up, the lorry that is described, the TAM 130 that you were driving in Pilica and Kula, was a lorry that belonged to Metalno, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I just want to clarify a few things about your war history. You were actually a mobilised soldier for about six months between 1992 and 1995, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: But of course. I was mobilised, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But the rest of the time, you were demobilised, you were working for Metalno as a driver throughout the whole of that three-year period, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I was working for Metalno, and that was part of my work obligation. I was occasionally called away when needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, I'll come back to that. Can we get to the day that you've told us about. Is it your recollection now that Radislav Pantic did not tell you the purpose for which you were sent to Pilica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: He assigned me to go to Pilica. He gave me a travel order and told me to drive soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And just so that we're clear, the days prior to that, had you been working for Metalno?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I was at the barracks as of the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, were you the only lorry driver that was sent to Pilica on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You've told us about some men in military uniforms you saw near to the Pilica cultural dom. I want to ask you this: They were unarmed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And during the course of that day, and I fully understand why, you had a lot of alcohol to drink, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, not that much, really, at the beginning. But later on, I drank.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you you couldn't do that during the course of the day?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: No, nobody told me anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I want to clarify one thing you said in your interview back in November. You said at one stage you ran away. Did you mean you ran away from the cultural dom at some stage during the day?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: No. I never entered the cultural hall, the dom, at any point. I didn't know what was in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey -- Mr. Haynes, if you could please repeat your question, because I don't think it got to the witness as it should. He's answered a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if I may, if there's -- if there's a specific cite to the interview transcript where there is a discussion of him running away, that might help as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'll move on for that -- from that. I may come back to it. It's not a particularly significant point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You were shown a document, and I'll show it to you again, by Mr. Thayer. It's P3227. Could we have that in e-court, please. Do you remember seeing that document a few minutes ago, when Mr. Thayer was asking you questions?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you understand what that document is and how it comes to be?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, these were probably the drivers who were part of the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But it's a document ordering your mobilisation, isn't it, on the 15th of December of 1994? Do you remember how long the task was you had to perform on the 15th of December of 1994; a day, two days, something like that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Believe me when I tell you that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But apart from the periods when you were lawfully mobilised, you worked for Metalno, didn't you? You were under their direction? The purpose of this order is to place you under somebody else's direction or command. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at another document of precisely the same nature, a bit more relevant; 7D722, please. Do you see this is a precisely similar document, dated the 15th of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go to page 5, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you see there are a list of people from your company, Metalno, at page 5, apparently mobilized on the 15th of July of 1995? Can it be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can it be scrolled down so he can see this, and the top of the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just for the record, when I briefly saw that first page, I think the date is actually the 17th of July. I stand to be corrected, but I saw something that said "17 July," not "15 July."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was both, both dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It was both. It's an order confirming those who are mobilised on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So can you read those numbered 127 to 142?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Am I supposed to read it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. Just tell me if you see your name there.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So it appears that whatever your former boss might have asked you to do, he didn't do it with any lawful authority, did he, Mr. Tomic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how it came about that he issued me this assignment, but from what I can see, the people listed under "Metalno" are not drivers, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tomic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Haynes. Ms. Nikolic, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two or three questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Tomic. My name is Jelena Nikolic, and I represent the Defence for Mr. Drago Nikolic. I have two or three questions to put to you in relation to the 17th of July 1995 and in relation to the events you've told us about today. You knew Mr. Drago Nikolic by sight from Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him, but not that well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You knew what he looked like?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the course of the 17th of July, when you were issued with the assignment at Standard, and later on in Pilica and in Branjevo, did you at any point see Drago Nikolic in any of these places?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you have any contacts with him?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TOMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. Just to confirm that none of the other Defence teams have any cross-examination. All right. Mr. Thayer, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Mr. Tomic, I told you in the beginning that we would finish with your testimony. We have even finished earlier than I expected, so you're free to go. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony, and on behalf of everyone, we wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exhibits. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, in addition to the three exhibits which were listed on our list of exhibits distributed a couple of days ago, I note first that 65 ter 295 is already in evidence, so we won't be offering that. But 3226 and 3227, PIC00200 and PIC00199, the latter two being pages from the transportation records, these do not need to be under seal, although the whole document previously was placed under seal. These particular selections can be made public, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections? Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll speak vicariously. No objection to that, and I don't imagine anybody else does. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. So these documents are admitted. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: 7D722, the mobilisation list for the 17th, relating to the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No objection, so that is admitted too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So it will be MFI'd for the time being, pending translation thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I do wonder whether that is really necessary. It's only a list of names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But why did you agree on the substance of the document, in other words, what kind of a document it is? I see no objection. I have no problem. Do you have a problem with MFI'ing it or, rather, admitting it rather than MFI'ing it?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, I don't, Mr. President. I'd always rather be safer than sorry and see the English translation, but I really have no objection to it coming in now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, we'll admit the document. If there are problems later on, will you please bring them to our notice and we can reverse the order and MFI it until a proper translation has been carried out. Okay. The next witness, Ewa Tabeau. Now, Defence counsel, please, going through your estimates, I notice that you have asked for an hour and 55 minutes. In reality, we had only considered an hour and a half, so you need to restrict yourselves to that. And then if there is justification for going beyond by a few minutes, we'll do what we did last time. Mr. Soljan, you have 30 minutes, and I hope you will keep within that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm the Presiding Judge, and I wish to welcome you to this Tribunal. It's very kind of you to come here at such short notice. We will be proceeding with your testimony straightaway and hopefully try and finish -- conclude today so that you can go home. Ms. Soljan will go first. She will be followed by the various Defence teams. But before you start giving evidence, you need to make the sacramental, solemn declaration that we have here, which you are being handed now. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us that you will be testifying the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. Please make yourself comfortable. Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Given the time constraint we have in presenting this witness's testimony, I just ask you for permission to just lead her on a few preliminary matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Permission granted under the usual conditions. If there is an objection, we'll go back on our permission.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I need a little help with the transcript. I can see it now, thank you. I didn't have the transcript. Now I have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. And if there are any problems with your headphones or anything else, please don't hesitate to let us know. Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Madam, please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I'm Ewa Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, you have submitted a CV titled "Professional Qualifications of Ewa Tabeau." Is this information in your CV up to date?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Not that I see it in front of me, but I'm speaking about the document I submitted together with the report, then yes it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: This the document dated 17th of December, 2007, and it's Exhibit 65 ter 3158. Now, you have a Ph.D. in mathematical demography from Warsaw School of Economics in Poland; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And you are a demographer by profession?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Since 2000, you've been working at the ICTY as project leader of the Demographics Unit?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And, briefly, what does your work in the OTP, in the Demographics Unit, entail?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: My work and the work of the unit is related to studying demographic consequences of the conflict -- 1990s conflicts in the former Yugoslavia, in particular in Bosnia and Herzegovina. As part of our responsibilities, we make -- I personally make expert reports for use in court, but there are also other responsibilities; for instance, maintaining information system on victims of the conflict, killed persons, missing persons, displaced persons, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned the writing of reports. Did you produce a report on 11 January 2008?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And if the usher could please place on e-court Exhibit 65 ter 3159.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Dr. Tabeau?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is the January 2008 report. This is the Srebrenica Missing 2007 Progress Report on the DNA-Based Identification by ICMP. That's the title of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And can you tell us what the purpose of this report was, please?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This report is an updated version of the report that was initially presented in November 2005. I'm referring to the report dated 21st of November, 2005.
