Similarly to the first report, this report as well summarises the statistics on the DNA-based identified persons related to the fall of Srebrenica in 1995. The report is made based on information provided by the International Commission for Missing Persons in Sarajevo, and that was the main source for this report. Well, this was perhaps the major goals, summarising the statistics on the identified persons. The second goal was, as well, cross-referencing the list of identified individuals provided by the ICMP in October 2007 with our OTP list of Srebrenica missing persons. By saying "our OTP list," I mean the list that was provided to this Trial Chamber and to Defence counsels in 2005, and Helge Brunborg testified in the beginning of 2007 about this list and the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you noted that you were cross-referencing the ICMP October 2007 list with our OTP list of Srebrenica missing persons. Were these your only sources in producing the report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, we basically used three lists for making the 2008 report. One was the 2005 OTP list of missing. The second was the 2007 ICMP list of the identified individuals. And in addition to this, we also studied a third list, the list of unique DNA profiles, also provided by ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could show on e-court, please, page -- or, rather, P03002A. And if there could be no broadcasting of this, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this list, Dr. Tabeau?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. This is the ICMP list of identified individuals, the main list which includes names of identified persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could just briefly move on to P03004A.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this list, Dr. Tabeau?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. This is the second list, the list of unique DNA profiles, also provided by ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And did you use this second list in the production of your most recent report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: We didn't. There are no names included in this list, so there is nothing that we could use in cross-referencing with other sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before we go on to summarising of the results of your report, could you please provide us with a brief summary -- or of the methodology used in producing your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The report -- the methodology used for producing this report is our standard methodology which was also used for our previous report, the 2005 report. Details of this methodology are discussed in the 2005 report. Basically, the methodology relates to, first of all, studying and assessing the quality of information that we used for our report and, secondly, in using the matching methodology for cross-referencing the lists. Well, matching methodology is basically comparing records from two lists using names of individuals and the date of birth, and by doing so, seeing whether there is a satisfactory degree of consistency between the compact records, and if there is so, there is a satisfactory degree of consistency, two records from two different lists can be declared as representing one and the same person.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: So specifically referring to the sources you were using to produce the report, what were the records you were actually using in your matching methodology?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: We were cross-referencing two lists; on one hand, the OTP list of 2005, the list of Srebrenica missing individuals, and, on the other hand, we were using the ICMP list of identified individuals. We were comparing some parts of information available in both lists in declaring matched records.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And, specifically, what type of information was this?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: As I said earlier, these were names, first name, father's name, family name of these individuals, and in addition to the names, also the date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, how did you control for duplications or how would you make sure that a person identified on one of your lists was not appearing multiple times?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, checking for duplicates is part of our standard procedure for assessment of sources. With regard to the 2005 OTP list of missing persons, we have done several thorough checks before the 2005 report was completed. With regard to the ICMP list, we have run several criteria. There is a list of this criteria, there were eight criteria used for running checks, duplicate checks. This list is discussed in the 2005 report, and so also in this case we used exactly the same criteria. One of the criteria was comparing duplicated names without looking at the date of birth, and of course later studying all available information about candidate duplicates. And having done this, we concluded there were no duplicated records in the ICMP file.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Were you also in contact with the ICMP regarding the information you obtained in October 2007 from the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. We saw that there were a number of deficiencies in the ICMP records. One of the deficiencies, perhaps the major one, was that a number of records reported by the ICMP represented three associations without the main case associated with them, so this was one of the problems. There were also other problems. Some deficiency protocols numbers, for instance, were seen. We contacted the ICMP and requested a clarification with regard to the deficient records and such a clarification was obtained shortly afterwards. Using the clarification, we were able to correct the affected records and to proceed with good data.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Dr. Tabeau, let me direct your attention to some of the major conclusions reached in your report, and this is at -- in your report, so 65 ter 3159, at page 3, ERN 0626-5767. In your report, Dr. Tabeau, you state that the total number of records in the ICMP update is 6.609. What does this number refer to?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is the overall total of all records in the ICMP file, one record representing one case, ICMP case. However, the 6.609 records don't represent the same number of individuals. This is related to the fact that the ICMP file contains two types of cases. The first type are main cases, representing different individuals. The second type are re-associations, that is, bone-to-bone matches. The main cases are, of course, positive DNA identifications that can be documented with associated protocol which -- whose number is available in the ICMP file.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us what the number of main cases was, according to your analysis?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The number of main cases is 4.263. This number represents different individuals in the ICMP file. This number should be seen as the number of individuals identified through the DNA analysis as of 4th of October, 2007. And the other records, the remaining records, that is 2.346, is the number of re-associations. These are records related to the main cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, the next number you mention is 3.837. Can you explain to us what this number means?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This number should be seen in the context of the 2005 OTP list of Srebrenica missing. On this list, we reported 7.661 individuals. The number of 3.837 names are records of identified persons reported by the ICMP, that at the same time also reported on the OTP list, 2005 OTP list of missing. This is simply the overlap of these two lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what percentage of the ICMP list were you able to match therefore with the OTP missing list?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This number represents 90 per cent of the ICMP records, and at the same time it represents about 50 per cent of the records of the missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And can you explain to us what happened with the remaining 10 per cent of the ICMP list?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The remaining 10 per cent, that is 426 records, are composed of two types of records. One type is a group of matches that we call "less-certain matches." That we call these matches less certain is related to the fact that what could be matched actually were only the names. The date of birth was unavailable to most of these records, either on the ICRC part or the ICMP part. So even though we saw the names appearing on the OTP list, we were unable to declare these matches as final matches. We -- in the future, perhaps, when the date of birth will become available for these individuals, we will be able perhaps to finalise the match matching. There were 261 such matches. It's perhaps important to note that the date of birth in the ICMP file is usually unavailable for records with multiple names. These names -- what I mean by that is in one record, for instance, three different first names, with the same father's name, for instance, and the same surname, and this simply means that ICMP, based on the information they have available, was unable to distinguish between these three individuals. The ICMP has, in many cases, three or two or four different DNA profiles, but is unable to associate the profiles with particular persons. In such cases, the date of birth is not reported. And in the ICRC data, also some dates of birth are unavailable, so in such cases the matching was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us about the remainder of the 10 per cent of the ICMP list?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The last group is 165 records. These are records that remain unmatched. We couldn't find these individuals on our OTP list of missing persons, and therefore we list them separately in our report, in our annex to our report. We consider these records as new and additional to the OTP list of Srebrenica missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Are there any other numbers in the executive summary that you refer to?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, there are a few other numbers. For instance, we refer to the statistics that were produced at some point in 2007 by Dean Manning. He also, in his report, gives some statistics on the identified persons. For instance, his number of individuals identified, and whose remains were exhumed from the sites he included in his report, is 3.252, and this is a number that is lower from the number we presented in our report. Well, there are certain differences in the approaches, his approach and our approach, and these can be explained. Basically, he has been very conservative, and he only worked with a number of gravesites related to Srebrenica, and to -- actually our approach was based on studying data, all data that were provided by the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that your report contained two annexes. Can we please have 65 ter 3159A on e-court, and if -- it's under seal. And, in particular, page 5 of this report -- of this annex. If there's a problem calling it up, I also have a hard copy. Dr. Tabeau, can you explain what this annex is, what this list represents?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is annex 2 of our report from January 2008. In annex 2, there are two parts. This particular page comes from part 1. Part 1 contains basically the records listed on the 2005 OTP list of Srebrenica missing. A large portion of information on this page is exactly as reported on the 2005 list of missing. By saying "large part," I mean all data items except for the two last columns. The two last columns are called protocol number of ICMP and the gravesite, and these two columns come from the ICMP data set provided to us in October 2007. Basically, this is what we see on this page. The rest is as reported in the 2005 OTP list of missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And can you please explain what it means when the last two columns do not have anything in them, in other words, when there is no protocol number and no gravesite indicated?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The blank cells mean that, in most cases, the persons have not yet been identified by the ICMP. In some cases, this also means that the persons might have been identified, but we were unable to match these records as definite matches and present the results on this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please have page 191 of this same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, can you explain briefly what this part of the annex represents?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is also annex 2 to our report, part 2 of the annex. This particular page lists -- includes records of additional individuals not reported on the OTP list of 2005, and this can be seen from the last column, where the status is indicated as a new name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And do you know why this name would not have appeared on the OTP -- 2005 OTP missing list, which for the record is P02414?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, it is possible that certain families reported their missing relatives to the ICMP and didn't report them to the ICRC. Well, from experience we know that there is no one-to-one relationship between different lists of missing persons. There is always a large -- a large common part, and none of the overlapping parts of these records would be no overlapping records reported only to the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Dr. Tabeau, you made reference to Mr. Manning's work, and did you participate in any way in the creation of his report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say we participated, but we were involved in this project. Our involvement was related mainly to reviewing the annexes to Dean Manning's report. As I said earlier today, there were a number of deficient records in the ICMP file that we clarified with ICMP and corrected later in our databases, so we were reviewing -- we had reviewed annexes to Dean Manning's report by checking whether the information he included in his report is all correct and doesn't contain any errors.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. And as a last question to you: Do you have an explanation as to why his number of total individuals found in ICTY gravesites of 3.252 together with 758 no-name profiles is different from your overlap of 3.837 individuals?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, it is different because his analysis is designed based on certain gravesites that he includes in his report. He only looks at gravesites that contained human remains exclusively related to Srebrenica. There were no mixed remains in these sites. These are sites known to ICTY and accepted by ICTY as such. And this is why his number is lower than the number we present in our report. I think it is from the ICMP data we can see that there were also a number of additional gravesites reported for identified individuals. It is possible that in some of them, the remains were mixed also from other episodes or incidents of the conflict. But we accepted all the ICMP data and used all of the data in our analysis in cross-referencing with the OTP list of missing. That's the difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. Who is going first? Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Ms. Tabeau. My make is Jelena Nikolic, and I appear on behalf of Mr. Drago Nikolic. I have a few questions for you, which I hope will make it easier for me to understand your approach to this report of 2005 and 2007. If I understood your testimony today well, the only source you used for your new report of the 11th of January of 2008 is the ICMP list which had been forwarded to you in October 2007. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is the only new source that was used.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the ICMP list is an official document which can be used to ascertain the identity of persons and to ascertain data on the death of those persons?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you mean by "an official," but it is certainly a document that is at some point shared with legal authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show P3002B, or 3D269. I think we have it in e-court under both of these designations. 3D269. I would ask that this document not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, I believe you are familiar with this letter. It was sent to the OTP by the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Does it state clearly that the list of October, the list of missing compiled by the ICMP, is secret, since there are still cases pending, awaiting confirmation by local authorities?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, this is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If I understood Mr. Parsons' testimony well -- excuse me. When a process of identification by DNA methods is concluded, such results are checked by anthropologists, pathologists, and other team members. At what point in time is the final death certificate issued ascertaining the identity of that person, the cause, manner and time of death?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It's a question, if he --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the procedure?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Only after the procedure has been completed, it is only then that we can consider a file or a case closed, and it is only then that we can receive the final death certificate ascertaining the fact that the person is deceased and the person's identity.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I believe you are right, but -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As a demographics expert, did you have any means to check the reliability of data and DNA analysis results from the ICMP lists?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, if you -- you're asking about me checking the quality of DNA matching and the methodology the ICMP uses for this, then the answer, is of course, no, this is not my area of responsibility and expertise, but I did check the quality of the statistical information of the -- reported in the ICMP file, and I can comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When going through the proofing that was done with you for this testimony, on the initial list compiled by the OTP of missing persons in Srebrenica in 2000, in your demographics office you used many more sources to come up with the final number of those who went missing that went beyond the sources mentioned to us now?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I wasn't involved in compiling the 2000 end list, but I'm aware of the 2000 report by Helge Brunborg and Henrik Urdal, and they just used the ICRC list of missing persons for compiling the list of missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they used both the census of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1991, as did you for your report of 2005. They used voters' lists from 1997 and 1998, the PHR base, database, and so on and so forth. Do you agree with me that those sources were used as well to make the reports of Helge Brunborg in 2005?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, these sources were also used, but the list, as such, was compiled mainly based on the ICRC lists of missing persons, several versions of the ICRC lists. The census, the voters' registers, were used so as to validate certain records selected, Srebrenica missing, and to eliminate possible survivors from the list of missing. And I should have mentioned PHR as the source of the list of missing. This list was used together with the ICRC list, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Or, rather, to determine the identity and to make sure that, to use the term "phantoms," did not appear on the list, people who actually never existed?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I just said. The census, voters' list, were used to eliminate survivors, if there were any, but from this point of view I don't think the approach we used for the 2005 list was different.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Concerning your report of the 21st of November, 2000 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Ms. Nikolic please repeat the exhibit number and the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, the interpreters would like the exhibit number and the date. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Thank you. The report of the 21st of November, 2005, Exhibit P2416, pages 9 and 10 in the B/C/S. In the English, it is pages 9 and 10. Exhibit 2416, that is fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You quoted the criteria -- you mentioned the criteria that you used for matching the names of individuals. I can wait for the entire text to appear. I think we have page 10 in the B/C/S. Can we go to the next page and to page 10 in the English version so that we could arrive at that part of the report. It is table 4. This is what I want to discuss. I wanted to ask you this: The five criteria are mentioned there, when it comes to matching, is that correct, or rather five keys, five criteria you used? First of all, if the names are similar. You had five autographic criteria; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, we used five criteria for matching, yes indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Out of which -- or let's say the fourth criterion is the first four letters --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Ms. Nikolic please quote at a slower pace.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will read out the criterion number 4 from your report. The first three -- first four letters, the first letter of father's name, year of birth, plus/minus five years.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Is that one of the criteria you used?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is, yes, for selecting candidate matches. It is not a criterion for declaring the true matches. It's a selection of candidates, potential possible matches.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: According to table 4, the number of possible and accepted matches, according to that criterion, out of 252 candidates, you have 249 accepted matches?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, this is -- this is what we read in table 4, and I would like to comment on this. For all these potential matches, we checked the records back in the census and compared whether there were more candidates -- more individuals with the same names and similar date of birth. And if there were not, we proceeded to declare a match. If there were more than one, we didn't declare a match. That was the procedure, first selecting candidate matches, assessing the matches by linking the records with the census information, and studying all available information about missing persons, and only then, after completing this procedure, making decisions about whether or not a potential match can be seen as a true match.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And so we have table number 4 in your report of the 21st November 2005; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, this is table number 4 in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you apply the other criteria for matching up to 71, which uses only initials of certain people to establish any possible matches? Perhaps we could show 3D142 to Ms. Tabeau so as to make my point clear, so that she could understand my question. Ms. Tabeau, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I am. This is, as the title says "Examples of Linking Criteria" for the census records with the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Those are the same criteria used by the OTP when matching names and data for individuals?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, these are particular criteria that were used in the matching of the census with the list of missing persons. I believe -- I don't remember which version of the missing persons list was it, but, well, these criteria were used. And of course similar criteria are used in matching other sources. The table we just discussed only lists five criteria, while the sources that are matched are also different, it is not the census, and only ICMP list, right, with the Srebrenica missing persons records. So it is not that we always used the same 71 criteria in any matching. This is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The five criteria we mentioned, can we use a statistical term? Could we call them keys used to establish matching?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what is the meaning of the word "keys" that you just used. Just five criteria, matching criteria, that we used to match two lists, the ICMP list and the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Criteria can be changed using the same sample and same material within the same statistical process. That is allowed, I presume.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, ideally, matching should be done on one numeric characteristic which is unavailable in the two lists that we were matching. In the absence of this one numerical characteristic, like personal identification number, there is a need to use alternative criteria. Alternative criteria, of course, on the first place must include names and the date of birth, and this is what we had available in both lists. This was the common part in the Srebrenica missing persons list and in the ICMP list of identified individuals. These common parts could be compared, and we did compare the parts by using the five criteria discussed in the 2005 report. That we didn't use 71, it can only mean that possibly we under-matched the two lists and "under-matched" means that the overlap of the two lists might be even bigger than we reported. That means that more identified persons were included in the OTP list, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to tell me this: Since you used the same criteria in your report of the 11th of January as well, we do not have any insight into what the degree of overlap there was in your latest report of the 11th of January, 2008, and the tables were not drawn up the same way they were in the report of the 21st of November, 2005. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: There is no such a table in the January 2008 report, but I can assure you that we used the same criteria. However, we've been more conservative this time in declaring true matches. That means that the less-certain matches that we included separately in this report might have been declared as final matches, that we did it too. That is the meaning of "under-matching," actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: However, we have no figures that would tell us something about the application, as you said yourself. As regards your report of the 11th of January, 2008, which is P3159, page 7 - could we please bring that up in e-court, 7 in B/C/S and 5 in English - it is table 1. It says: "Review of Type of Information" or "Overview of Data Items Provided in the October 2007 Update of ICMP, on DNA-Based Identifications of Srebrenica Victims." Below the table, I believe you have it in English, you say: "Date and place of disappearance are both related to the fall of Srebrenica." The date of disappearance has one value for all identified persons related to the fall of Srebrenica. "The 11th of July, 1995," in quotation marks, disregarding the actual date of disappearance or death of victims. "We therefore did not use the date of disappearance in any analysis." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: When it comes to date of disappearance as reported by ICMP, we didn't, because of -- for the reason that you mentioned. The ICMP is not interested in things like data of disappearance or place of disappearance. They do the DNA matching and identification, and this is what is the crucial part of information for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: During Mr. Parsons' testimony, we were told that they entered the date of disappearance as received from the families of those disappeared. Therefore, such data was unreliable.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: As far as I know, they just created this item based on the information from the relatives, but it doesn't mean that the relatives provided exact date of disappearance. They provided information about whether or not a person went missing in the fall of Srebrenica of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What source did you use based on which you established that the victims went missing in the duration of 1994 and in relation to the events in Srebrenica, having in mind your report and what you've just said?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, we used the ICRC list of missing persons version of 2005. This is the source that we used for the compilation of our 2005 list of Srebrenica missing. So the date of disappearance that is presented in the annex, annex 2 to our January report, comes as originally reported by ICRC in their list and as reported in our report of 16th November 2005.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And it made its way on to the ICRC list based on the information provided by the families and based on the questionnaires that were filled out for every missing person?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I believe that that's the source for the date of disappearance reported by ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, how many of those who went missing on the OTP list, for whom you claim went missing in 1995, actually had the date of disappearance or death going back to 1992, 1993, or 1994?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, when it comes to the persons listed on the OTP list, the date of disappearance was the criterion as to whether to include a person in this list or not, so I'm pretty sure that there are no 1992s, 1993s, 1994s. It is all 1995, July to December 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you compare this OTP list with the list of ABiH soldiers, such as found in the archives of the demographics department of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No, we didn't. This is a list of missing from Srebrenica, so if a soldier would be missing, it would be still a missing person on the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show a Defence exhibit to the witness. It is 3D -- I'll try to use the shorter version, Your Honours, since I have two versions, but I'm trying to steer clear of long lists. It could be 3D299. This document contains two pages. Could we have both documents on the screen at the same time so that Ms. Tabeau could compare.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document to appear, I think, Ms. Tabeau, that you are convinced that the demographics team of the Defence worked at the OTP in 2007, at their premises, and you provided a number of documents to them which they used in their demographic analyses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, there was a Defence team in 2007 working with the sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to their findings, we now have these two tables. The upper one is a list of the OTP. Below, we have a list and examples from ABiH database. I apologise. I did not ask to go into private session, but in any case this should not be broadcast, and I'll try to avoid mentioning any names. In the first column, according to your OTP list on the 13th of July, we have those who went missing in Kamenica, according to the official data of the Army of B and H that the OTP has in its archives. The same person went missing on the 10th of January, 1994, as a member of the ABiH for unknown -- with an unknown cause of death in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, is it a question? This is what it says here in this table.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: There are nine such examples here of individuals who are listed on the OTP list as missing, as victims who went missing in Srebrenica in 1995, who, according to the official BH Army records, which you have in your possession, went missing prior to 1995 in other areas, and to be precise in the period between 1992 and 1995. How could you compile a list without consulting that source first?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, you might not know this, but in his 2000 report, Helge Brunborg wrote that he was asked to compile a list of missing from Srebrenica. This was his task, and this is what he did and what we followed up on. While we didn't cross-reference this list with fallen soldiers or other sources unknown, that is because it is not a list of known deaths and missing persons. Our OTP list is a list of missing persons and exclusively missing persons. In the example you are showing here, I see that the cause of death, at least for the cases that I see on the screen, is unknown or missing. This might mean that the date of disappearance is the date that these individuals were last seen. This does not contradict the fact that the persons later died during the fall of Srebrenica, so that is one observation. The second observation is that, well, I believe there were a number of inconsistencies in the lists of military personnel fallen during the war, and I remember at some point we contacted the Ministry of Defence and asked for a clarification on a number of cases, not in the context of our project on the Srebrenica missing list, but in the context of other projects, and corrections were provided to us, and dates of this kind, 1993, 1994, were corrected to be 1995. So this is why I believe it would be necessary to first try to obtain a clarification of these cases from the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to declare the cases as inconsistent on the OTP list.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Madam Tabeau, you believe that the OTP list, based on the raw DNA data, is more reliable than the BH Army records, in terms of the dates of death and the years of death, which you also ascertain on the basis of an individual's statement as to the time of disappearance?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that ICMP data is very reliable, and the selection of the records for the list they provided us was based on studying the sites, gravesites, whether or not the sites were related to the fall of Srebrenica. And in addition to this, they also have in their databases information from the relatives of the missing persons, and from this source they can see whether or not individuals were reported as missing during the fall of Srebrenica. So it is like a double-check they use to compile the list of identified persons related to Srebrenica. That is the reason for me to believe that this is a very reliable source.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you told us that the ICMP was not interested in the date of disappearance or the date of death, that they were only dealing with DNA analyses?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is very correct. I don't obtain date of disappearance and place of disappearance from the ICMP, but through linking of sources on the individual level. The information about the place and time of disappearance is available as reported to the ICRC, also by a reliable source, by the relatives of the missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that it is time for a break, and I'll only have a couple of questions left before I finish my examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I -- thank you, madam. May I have an indication from the other Defence teams, Mr. Zivanovic or Madam Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was supposed to examine Madam Tabeau. I asked for some 15 minutes. However, Madam Nikolic has already exhausted some topics I wanted to deal with, and it is quite possible I will have no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We adopt the same position. We've reserved 15 minutes, but we'll look at it and hopefully we'll have no questions of Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we reserved 15 minutes, but I believe that I'll be able to complete my cross-examination for five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Gvero and Pandurevic, I take it no cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: We don't have questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall do our utmost to finish with your testimony, madam, today. Thank you. Twenty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please call up document 3D02 [as interpreted]. And before Madam Tabeau is shown the document, I have one question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the letter that was sent to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, could counsel repeat the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D302, the letter from the Federal Commission on Missing Persons, Mr. Masovic, dated the 28th of December, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the letter and with the exchange that the OTP had with the Bosnian authorities or, rather, the local authorities in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with this letter. And regarding the exchange, I don't -- I don't know what are you talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: "Exchange" is what I said, the exchange of letters and not the extent. But please look at page 1 of the letter, where Mr. Masovic informs the OTP about the number of victims that were exhumed -- found and exhumed from the service in 2007. Since your findings partially rely on those of Mr. Manning, I wanted to know if you were aware of this figure of 929 exhumed individuals, 474 of whom were identified in the area where the column was moving.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I -- first of all, not seeing the entire letter, just the first few lines of the letter, but from the first lines I already can see I'm unaware of this letter, I haven't seen the letter. And if these statistics you mentioned come from the letter or related materials, that I must say I'm unaware of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the break, whilst we were discussing the soldiers who were killed and who were listed on the BH Army records, which contains detailed information in relation to each and every one of them, including the personal identification number, you'll agree with me that these lists originate from the files of the Office of the Prosecutor, do they not?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, the source is the Ministry of Defence of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but I think that these records, it was my impression, were extracted from this source. But you know better than me what was the -- what of the three lists was used. And we have the list of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina in our office, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Which refer to 30.000 soldiers killed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: About 28.000 names were reported, with a few duplications, in the federal list. This is only one of the three lists. There are two more, VRS and HVO have their own lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: These lists, in statistical and demographic terms, contain all the data, first and last names, father's name, personal identification numbers, and so on and so forth; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: They do include the data items you mentioned and some information such as cause of death and place of death or disappearance -- sorry place is not included. Date of death is included, not place of death or disappearance. And some other items as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Those were the lists we discussed previously and which you said Mr. Brunborg did not consult while compiling his November 2005 report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, this is what he didn't use. He didn't use a number of other sources that report on the so-called known deaths, the most important ones being the database on wartime deaths of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina with altogether 75.000 records, and another one of the RS authorities with 65.000 records, and this is related -- the purpose of the Brunborg project and all following projects was compiling the list of missing from Srebrenica. This list shouldn't be seen as a complete source of information on all individuals that were killed or disappeared in the fall of Srebrenica. It is just the list of missing persons, and of course some dead persons as well, but those dead were first reported as missing to the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: These sources which you mention were not consulted, had they been consulted, the nine cases we looked at indicate that there is a large number of individuals who died before 1995 and who nevertheless got it on to the OTP list of persons related to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Of course, it is not true that a large number of individuals on the OTP -- any number of individuals on the OTP list are reported as dead in earlier years, not in 1995. Well, I don't know, how can you draw this conclusion based on nine cases of which you are absolutely uncertain as to the quality of reporting of information? And, yeah, this is, I think, a very misleading conclusion. You may not do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. Those were only nine illustrations, and there is over a hundred such cases. But let me continue with my examination. When you were drafting your 11 January 2008 report, were you, as a demographer, duty-bound to use, except for the raw ICMP list, also the official sources such as the records of death by relevant official bodies?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I don't understand what are relevant official bodies, but this is perhaps not so important. The purpose of the whole exercise was to cross-reference the OTP list of missing with the records of the identified persons of the ICMP, and this is what we did in this report, and this is what we present in terms of statistics and some basic demographic distributions in the January 2008 report. So we didn't have the purpose of including any source available or unavailable, just the list of identified persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In other words, you did not use the minutes ascertained in the death of the Cantonal Courts of Tuzla, Zenica, and so on and so forth, all those documents; you only used individual segments that are normally used, but only some of them of those that are normally used to ascertain the death of a given individual? For instance, a copy of the register, this is something that I would consider an official source.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. I can only repeat: We wanted to cross-reference missing list of OTP of 2005 with the DNA-based identifications of the ICMP, and this is what we did and this is what we presented. Perhaps you can rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you consult the clinical -- the voters' registers of 2006 [as interpreted], perhaps, to ascertain that the lists match, or was the purpose of your exercise merely to make the ICMP list an official one?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, what is register of 2006, we don't --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I apologise. It wasn't entered into the transcript properly. What I meant was the 2006 voters' registers of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, as you know, from the 2005 report on the list of Srebrenica missing, we did use, when compiling the list of missing of 2005, the population census, three voters' registers, 1997, 1998 and the 2000 register, and we used SOL records of the internally displaced persons and refugees of 2000, the official register of these individuals, in order to eliminate possible survivors from the OTP list of missing. But once the list was finished, we didn't do much work on it, any work on it, we just used the list as it was compiled in 2005 for the purpose of cross-referencing the list with the latest ICMP list of identified persons. So, in fact, in some way, these voters' registers, registers of IDPs and refugees, the census, are all there, are all there, through the OTP list of missing, but not that we used these sources in the context of the ICMP data. Why would we be doing this? This all has been done already.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Your 11 January 2008 report does not contain a full demographic portrayal of the situation. It merely serves to make official the ICMP list?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, there are two things. The January 2008 report is a full report, because it discussed what we wanted to and planned to discuss in this report. That's one thing. Second, we don't need to make the ICMP official -- ICMP data official. I don't know still what does this mean to you, "official." The ICMP list contains cases of identified persons with important reference numbers to the main identification report. That would be the protocol ID number available from this list, with the case number available, which is the label attached to the remains. It includes as well ICMP identification number. So through all these IDs and the name of the person, you have a complete record of information about the identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Ms. Nikolic and witness, we are repeating ourselves over and over again. I think we can move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So Madam Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just have a couple of minutes, if the Court allows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Tabeau, again.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Ma'am, today on page 61, line 25, you spoke, in answers to my colleague, Madam Nikolic, regarding the criteria of plus/minus five. Do you remember that, basically?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, we discussed the five years limit at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me the source of that standard that you used the criteria of plus/minus five?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, the source should be seen as our expertise in matching and comparing related records, and another source is the fact that dates of birth are reported not always in a reliable way. This is what we know from the ICMP, but this is also our observation, our own observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right. Actually, my question was a bit different, and it was probably my fault. What my question is: Is this a standard that's typically utilised internationally or is this a standard that you, yourself, have set, this five plus-or-minus criteria that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, if you expect that I will give you international guidelines published on these particular five years, then I must disappoint you. There is no such a published standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So when I say -- asked you what sources there are, those are just internal sources that you've utilised, and you don't -- they're not used in any other nation, country, which deal with demographics or the study of displaced or missing persons; is that really what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No, this is not what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, help me and describe for me which other entities or organisations use this criteria, specifically.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I think generally the matching as a method is a well-recognised standard, and in many countries, like, for instance, Scandinavian countries, who don't have the population census, matching is an important way of collecting information about the individuals, the population, and compiling statistics. Matching, in that case, would be based on individual identification, numbers, as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right. And I'm familiar with that methodology of matching, Dr. Tabeau. My specific question is -- and if you can't help us, I'll move on to another point. Is the criteria of utilising this plus or minus five?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I explained earlier, there are no written published on plus or minus five years. This limit can be established based on the study of the data and based on your own assessment of deficiencies, in particular, in this case, in the date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that, and I'll move on in the interests of time. I want to know, when you said that you relied on the ICMP reports, if you could qualify that for me. Did you rely on all their reports or some of them? And if some of them, which ones, if I can put that compound question in the interest of time to you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what you mean "with the ICMP reports." We used a list of identified persons that was provided by the ICMP, right, for --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me then restate it, if I may, and I apologise for cutting you off, Doctor. If you utilised the data from the ICMP, as opposed to reports, so we'll just change the word to "data," did you use all their data or part of their data?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, they provided us with a subset of data on -- related to the identified persons related to the fall of Srebrenica, but I also do the DNA identifications for many other victims that would cover not only victims of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina but also Kosovo, for instance, and in some cases Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you used part of their data; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, we used part of their data.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, all I'm interested to know, Doctor, is: What part didn't you utilise in providing your report of January 2008? If you could list that out, if you know.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, what are -- I didn't use the data that were unrelated to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Anything else that you didn't use from the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Like what, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Like all the data that you were provided by them, you took everything that relates to Srebrenica, everything else you didn't utilise. So with respect to Srebrenica, you were provided with all that data, and you used all that data to come up with your report; would that be a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: They provided a separate list for Srebrenica. It's a separate data set, a subset of all the data they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's all you utilised; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, in this particular report, yes. In the previous report, we - addition to the Srebrenica list of ICMP - used the notice, the so-called ICMP notice, which is much broader.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, that's all I have, Doctor. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Madam Tabeau. My name is Aleksandar Lazarevic, and I will ask some questions of you on behalf of General Borovcanin. Could we please see 03159A on e-court, and I would kindly ask that the document not be broadcast, since it is under seal. Let us go to page 20 of the document immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honours, I would kindly ask for some guidelines, because this document is under seal and I, in my cross-examination, I intend to reference to some particular date from this document. Whether we should revert to private session, it contains particular names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move to private session, because I don't know what document this is, and perhaps -- are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we have concluded your cross-examination, Madam Tabeau, which means you're free to go. Thank you so much for having come over to give testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Soljan, exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That would be 65 ter numbers 3158, 3159, as well as 3159A, 3004 and 3004A, and 3006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections? We hear none. Admitted. Documents for the Drago Nikolic Defence? Ms. Nikolic, you have three documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, of according to the list that was forwarded, it was 3D299, 3D142, and 3D302. The other documents I used have already been put on the Prosecution's list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Other Defence teams wish to object? None. So these three documents are admitted. Mr. Lazarevic, I suppose the ones you used are already in the records, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's all been tendered into evidence by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that concludes our business for today. I wish to thank you for your cooperation. Tomorrow, you have the last witness, Mr. McCloskey. Don't tell me she's not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: She's here, and that is the last witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, all right. So we'll deal with her testimony tomorrow, and then perhaps after that we'll deal with the residues of the Butler exhibit list, of course, without prejudice to what we discussed earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and we are working on some old stipulations from long ago and a few other items which we may need to alert you to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, while we still have some more time, we would like you to get together, and also with the Registrar, to clean up for us the slate on which we have put so many documents, marking them for identification. Then we need you, particularly, Mr. Ostojic, we need you to conclude for us, in a clear way, clear manner, all issues -- pending issues, if there are any left, relating to the aerial images. As I see it, but of course I stand to be corrected, it seems that there is a standing on your part, Mr. Ostojic, but all other issues, pre-existing issues, have been solved, but the objection stands. But if I am wrong, please correct me tomorrow. Some time back, Mr. McCloskey, you had informed us, in relation to the Skorpion video, that you were having talks, discussions, with the Defence teams and that you were in the process of finalising a stipulation. I don't know at what stage you have arrived, but if perhaps tomorrow you could articulate this. I think for the time being, that is all. There are some other issues, but I need to discuss them with my colleagues before I raise them, if at all, tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
